articles.title: Islamabad High Court judge questions legal status of Afghan students
articles.description: ISLAMABAD: The Islamabad High Court has raised important legal questions over the maintainability of a constitutional petition seeking extension of visas for 87 Afghan students currently residing in Pakistan on student visas. Justice Khadim Hussain Soomro raised questions regarding the legal status of the Afghan students as well as the authority of their lawyer to represent them before the court. During the hearing, the judge questioned the petitioner’s counsel about the circumstances in which the Afghan students were allowed to enter Pakistan and whether similar treatment could be sought by students from other countries. “Sir, we are currently at war with the Afghans. If Indian students come, will you allow them to come too?” Justice Soomro asked the counsel. The lawyer submitted that the 87 Afghan students had arrived in Pakistan in 2023, when, according to him, the national policy regarding Afghan students was different. Justice Soomro observed that the petition had been filed under the constitutional jurisdiction of the high court and questioned whether the Constitution provided Afghan nationals with a right to invoke such jurisdiction. The counsel argued that the students had entered Pakistan on valid student visas for a period of one year and that their presence in the country had been permitted by the government. The judge then questioned the authority under which the lawyer had obtained power of attorney from the 87 Afghan students. “Under which law have you taken power of attorney from these 87 Afghan students?” Justice Soomro asked. The court also suggested that the students should approach the Afghan embassy in connection with their matter instead of seeking relief through the constitutional jurisdiction of the Islamabad High Court. “You should go to the Afghan embassy and your case will be heard there. The Afghan embassy will contact the Pakistani embassy,” the judge remarked. The petitioner’s counsel said that he would assist the court on the legal questions raised during the proceedings. The case concerns the extension of visas of 87 Afghan students who came to Pakistan in 2023 to pursue their studies. The petitioners have sought relief regarding their continued stay in Pakistan following the expiry or impending expiry of their student visas. The court subsequently adjourned further hearing of the case. Published in Dawn, August 29th, 2026

articles.title: CBAM trade barriers
articles.description: WHILE Pakistan struggles with the accumulated cost of climate inaction and finds international climate finance elusive, it must now confront an emerging challenge: trade barriers priced according to the carbon embedded in each exported product. The false comfort that this does not touch our key exports to the EU and UK has deferred reforms, with the cost growing steeper by the day. Contradictory policy, misusing carbon levies instead of building a domestic Emissions Trading System (ETS), has made trade even harder. Since January 2026, EU importers of steel, cement, aluminium, fertilisers and electricity have had to buy certificates for the carbon embedded in their imports, with the first annual declarations due next year. Direct exposure under these sectors is small for Pakistan — roughly 1.2 per cent of total exports, typically a percentage easy to ignore. CBAM (Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism), however, is a serious warning. On March 9, 2023, my column on ‘Trade and climate adaptation’ in this paper flagged that Pakistan would need to build carbon labelling and export competitiveness around it, not wait it out. As I wrote then, “they are expected to shift demand towards less carbon-intensive products”. Some three years later, in January 2026, my argument turned from a warning to heed to an opening to seize, urging that CBAM “should be seen as an incentive to accelerate our own decarbonisation”. Two columns, three years apart — but one constant: Pakistan’s institutions have moved slower than the mechanism they were warned about. Pakistan’s exports to the EU reached $8.86 billion in FY25, up from $8.24bn the year before, with textiles, which accounted for the largest share of that total, driving the growth. That concentration has real addresses: major textile houses in Faisalabad, Lahore and Karachi — employing thousands of workers and supplying top brands in the EU — are directly exposed in the coming scope expansion. Pakistan’s economic set-up is structured to fund CBAM via citizens’ fuel bills while getting no credit. In the sectors that CBAM already covers, the exposure affects heavy industry: leading domestic cement makers supply most of that sector’s output, with the steel mills in Karachi making up the remainder. The disproportionately higher share, however, sits in textiles, concentrated in three industrial cities that would absorb the shock first. Pakistan already collects carbon levies. CBAM allows a deduction: a home-country carbon price already paid can be subtracted from the EU’s border levy. It is the mechanism’s one window of opportunity — a domestic carbon price that is real, product-linked and verifiable. Pakistan’s misplaced levies cannot qualify because they aren’t earmarked; the revenue funds the deficit, not the industries that generated it. They are regressive, taxing fuel and transport consumption rather than signalling to producers. And they carry no product-level accounting, so a generalised fuel levy tells Brussels nothing about the carbon intensity of a bale of cotton yarn or a tonne of billet steel. Without that link, CBAM won’t recognise it as a carbon price. The cost will fall twice: first domestically into a levy that does nothing for decarbonisation, and then again at the EU border into a certificate purchase. Pakistan’s economic set-up is structured to fund CBAM out of its own citizens’ fuel bills while getting zero credit for it. The Securities and Exchange Commission has draft ESG [Environmental, Social, and Governance] Disclosure Guidelines and the State Bank is building a national Green Taxonomy. The taxonomy lets a bank tell a green loan from an ordinary one; the guidelines let an auditor certify emissions rather than estimating them. Without both at scale, product-level Monitoring, Reporting and Verification (MRV) data has nowhere credible to be recorded, and any domestic carbon price has no verified base to attach to. On domestic ETS, the story is older still. In 2018, the climate ministry commissioned a UNFCCC-backed study recommending an ETS for the country’s largest power and industrial emitters — roughly 168 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent. It was never built. What arrived instead was the Carbon Market Policy Guidelines of 2024, aiming at a different problem — a framework for selling carbon credits to international markets under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, generating revenue from offset projects sold abroad while pricing no carbon at home. Six years after its own study told it what to build, the ministry built something adjacent, and the follow-up never came. No ministry can close this gap alone. Commerce defends market access and negotiates recognition of any domestic carbon price with Brussels. The climate ministry owns the ETS architecture. Industries and production, and finance and revenue carry the implementation weight, ie, audits with textile associations and SMEs, and the decision on whether levies are earmarked. Energy determines whether industrial power and its transmission are clean and cheap enough to matter on a factory floor. A CBAM strategy that lives in a single ministry’s file will not meet the deadline. Fixing this requires no new instrument, only the one Pakistan was already told to build, made legible to the mechanism that is about to tax us anyway. First, earmark a fixed share of carbon and climate levy proceeds by law for a dedicated decarbonisation fund to derisk investments. Second, revive the 2019 ETS design-and-build accredited MRV infrastructure at the product level. Third, sequence deliberately: taxonomy and baseline audit first; verification capacity second; financing (concessional green refinance, green sukuk against industrial assets) third; and only then mandatory disclosure. Get the order wrong, and Pakistan builds compliance infrastructure for a carbon price that still doesn’t exist. None of this is unusual by regional standards. Vietnam did not wait; it used its own EU trade agreement to force pilot emissions trading and SME carbon accounting. Indonesia offers the opposite lesson: a loan-financed energy transition, where debt is now carried alongside the carbon bill — a trap that Pakistan’s fiscal space cannot sustain. The choice facing Islamabad is not whether to pay for carbon; that was decided before the levies were introduced. The choice is whether that payment counts for anything, at home or in Brussels. Right now, it counts for nothing in either place. September 2027 is when this stops being an abstraction and becomes an invoice, priced at EU default values unless Pakistan shows its own numbers by then. The levies can do double duty. There is not enough time left to pretend that 1.2pc is the whole story. The writer is a climate expert. Published in Dawn, August 29th, 2026

articles.title: FBI changes policy on applicants' experience with prostitution
articles.description: The FBI is no longer treating an applicant’s prior encounters with prostitutes as an automatic bar against employment. The change comes amid broader concerns about a loosening of recruitment requirements at the nation’s premier federal law enforcement agency. The bureau still intends to dismiss applicants who are revealed during the vetting process to have engaged in prostitution within the last 10 years, three or more times overall or while in a position of trust. That’s according to guidance issued this spring and described by a person familiar with the matter. For others, it will allow for consideration of the context of the conduct rather than treat it as grounds for an automatic rejection from the FBI’s hiring process.

articles.title: Kiss-cam scandal brewing in Lyons Township between elected officials
articles.description:
Earlier this year, Lyons Township Clerk Elyse Hoffenberg, a Democratic candidate for Cook County Board, pushed for the installation of surveillance cameras at her Countryside government office at taxpayer expense.

Footage from those cameras is now at the center of a bizarre political and legal dispute that’s becoming a campaign issue in Hoffenberg’s race — leading her to make accusations of extortion and dirty politics, while others question whether she used public property for private purposes and is lashing out to try to tamp down a scandal.

At the center of it: Video images showing Hoffenberg getting kissed by Bridgeview Mayor Steve Landek, a former state senator who is Lyons Township’s Democratic committeeman, after hours at the township office on July 13.

Hoffenberg’s Republican opponent in the County Board race, former Cook County Commissioner Liz Gorman, says she fielded a tip that there might be something incriminating on the video system, so she filed an open-records request for a copy.

Under state law, government records are generally accessible to members of the public upon request to a public agency, whether written documents, emails or images, and the like.

Gorman, of Orland Park, says she still hasn’t gotten everything she requested from the township. But under increasing pressure, Hoffenberg, who lives in La Grange with her family, released images to select media, along with a written statement that said:

“Today, in the interest of transparency, I am releasing a video clip publicly that has generated some attention. My political opponents attempted to extort me regarding this video, saying they would drop their threats to release it if I end my campaign. I am certain that our community will find this kind of old school politics of harassment abhorrent, and I won’t be bullied.”

“While the video lacks proper context to make it clear what is happening, what it shows is a lighthearted, friendly and non-romantic moment among colleagues,” though she previously described the kiss, according to an online account by Patch, “as a peck and said she told the mayor it was inappropriate, prompting him to apologize.”

Her public statement released Friday adds: “I am staying focused on my campaign to bring strong leadership to this community, and I look forward to continuing this work.”

Gorman said she was not involved in any harassment or extortion, and that her attorney submitted a letter to the township asking that any video not be deleted.

“Nobody talked to her, nobody visited her,” Gorman said. “Extortion — that’s a pretty strong accusation, but when you don’t have the facts you go to lying, and pointing figures and not looking in the mirror.”

Gorman says the issue is not really the kiss, but rather her opponent’s judgment in using a government office for seemingly private matters.

Hoffenberg wouldn’t answer questions, and she’s accused Lyons Township Supervisor Chris Getty — the mayor of Lyons who’s running as an independent for Congress to replace U.S. Rep. Jesus “Chuy” Garcia (D-Ill.) in the U.S. House — of leaking the video to Gorman and also trying to delete the video.

A lawyer representing Getty on governmental and political fronts, Burt Odelson, says neither of those claims is true.

There's been talk by some township officials about hiring a politically connected Chicago law firm to investigate the matter, potentially at taxpayer expense, but it's unclear whether that will happen.
